title: Sacred theology considers principles and parts; a principle is incomplex or complex
english: Chapter 2. On the principles of sacred theology, and specifically on the first and last complex principle.
I. Sacred theology asks us to weigh two things: the principles from which the discipline is drawn, and the parts into which it is divided.

II. By principles of sacred theology we mean those propositions that let us deduce the sacred dogmas of the Christian faith by ordered discourse — and then resolve the deduced dogmas back into the same propositions — so that a sound, modest, God-fearing person may rightly give assent.

Taken generally, a principle is whatever something proceeds from in any way (Thomas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 33, art. 1). Principles are either simple or complex. A simple principle is a simple term, either principal or less principal. The principal term is God himself — which is to say, Christ — of whom ([[1 Corinthians 1:30 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 1:30]]) speaks. Fulgentius writes to Thrasamund (p. 108): Christ is the beginning, for as everlasting he goes before; Christ is the end, for as perpetual he closes all things. Christ is the beginning, for he himself began; Christ is the end, for he perfects. The less principal term is the Word of God, the instrument through which the Holy Spirit converts, illuminates, and saves ([[Romans 1:16 >> Bible:Romans 1:16]]; compare 1 Corinthians and related places).

With those two incomplex principles in place, we turn to the first complex principle: a whole proposition from which a conclusion follows by logic. Some therefore call it a logical principle, or a principle of cognition, because our logical deduction of what we believe starts here, and demonstration cannot climb beyond this first and most general point. The complex principle holds together two respects at once — the respect from which, namely God's infallible testimony, and the respect under which, namely the light of revelation — and so is called a principle from which and under which. That sets it far apart from an exterior principle, which only occasions our knowledge of faith and is a necessary condition without which faith does not arise (today, for example, the parental authority that plants saving truth in us: [[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]), and also far apart from a motive principle, which is only a topical or probable argument, such as a miracle.

A Christian does not depend on those lesser supports. They win only the assent of human apprehension — Bellarmine himself grants as much. What then is our principle? It is apodictic and indemonstrable, worthy of faith from itself, and such that falsehood cannot underlie it in any way. Still, a necessary condition must be joined to it — hearing or reading — which is why Scripture calls it the word of hearing ([[1 Thessalonians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Thessalonians 2:13]]). I am speaking of the dogmas of faith as they reach us from outside. Dogmas come in two kinds: some for believing, others for knowing. The first kind is known by God's special revelation; the second lies open under the light of reason. The first is believed; the second is known. Our subject here is properly the former. Propositions that do not properly belong to faith — and some such do appear in the Bible — fall outside this account.

title: The first and last principle of sacred theology is authentic and self-attesting
english: III. Among these principles one stands first and last; another hangs from that first principle and is ranked beneath it.

The distinction matters most under the Smyrnaean, Pergamene, Thyatiran, and above all the Sardian church-condition in which we now live. The Ephesian condition still had one principle alone — the written Word of God ([[Acts 28:25 >> Bible:Acts 28:25]]). Augustine praised that same character under the Pergamene state: Let us use the liberty to which the Lord has called us. As for those men whose praise we dare not equal, whose writings we refuse to set beside many Scriptures, whose genius we love, whose speech delights us, whose charity we admire, and whose martyrdoms we revere — whatever they thought otherwise, we must not receive it as canonical. We do them no injury when we mark off any saying or writing of theirs from the canonical authority of the divine Scriptures.

IV. Sacred theology's first and last principle is the one that, once granted, lets every other dogma of faith be deduced, while it itself is not deduced directly from any other — and therefore deserves to be called authentic and autopiston, self-attesting.

We name it first and last because Christian theological discourse cannot go beyond it without sliding into an infinite regress or a circle, and both paths are vicious. The proof runs in six steps. (1) Whatever is known is either a principle or a conclusion; philosophy already teaches that. In theology's dogmas concerning divine and eternal life, just as in other disciplines, we move from one point to another and prove one claim by arguing from another. (2) Those proofs and conclusions must halt in something first that is not itself proved from elsewhere — otherwise they circle or stretch to infinity, both of them faults. (3) First here means first for the Christian person's knowledge. (4) We are not requiring the principles of being and the principles of knowing to be identical everywhere; theology's own character often refuses that identity. God is author and principle of being for the whole creation. Yet our question is how it becomes established for us that God created all things. (5) Still more: the question is less how the point might be proved to this or that hearer, and more how it stands firm for the Christian — and on what he, who neither spins in a circle nor rushes on like a madman into infinity, is finally founded insofar as he is and is called a Christian. (6) Because we are asking for a principle ordered to our cognition, and for one from which further claims can be deduced by discourse, what we seek is plainly the complex principle that Aphorism 2 already named an axiom: an examined, proposed, authentic, autopiston principle.

title: Two kinds of discipline; assent in the first rests on the dictate of right reason
english: 7. Here we take as settled that disciplines the human mind can grasp fall into two kinds. One stands under the light of reason. The other — once reason's light is already presupposed and set in its apt place for use — is known under the light of faith, that is, of divine revelation.

8. In the first kind, the ground of assent is the dictate of right reason. By that phrase we do not mean the rational soul itself, or the human intellect as such. That the intellect can err and be deceived — and often is, even in the wisest of mortals — no one doubts. Nor does it stumble only in matters of faith, where it must trip forever unless the Holy Spirit guides and Scripture holds the torch. It also errs, and often, in civil affairs and in the practical business of this life.

9. So "right reason" here is not an intellect that never errs or strikes against anything. It is only the intellect's right judgment about a matter that is either known by nature or follows by legitimate inference from naturally known principles. That remaining judgment after the fall — however much of it is left in us — is what we call right reason: theoretical when it judges theoretical things, practical when it judges practical things.

10. Whenever people say that right reason teaches this or that, or that something agrees with right reason, they mean that the claim is true and certain — either because it is a principle known by nature, or because it can be drawn from such a principle by sound consequence. Right reason, then, is nothing other than true judgment about what natural principles let us know.

11. Many today misuse the word "reason" on its worse side, as if it meant only human corruption. Scripture regularly takes it in the good sense ([[Romans 12:1 >> Bible:Romans 12:1]]; [[Romans 2:15 >> Bible:Romans 2:15]]; compare [[1 Peter 2:1 >> Bible:1 Peter 2:1]]). So Gregory Nazianzen, in Oration 2 on theoretical reason: Reason, he says, is given us by God, innate in all, and is so far the first law inhering in everyone that by contemplating what falls under sight it leads us to God. Augustine, On Free Choice of the Will II.18: You look at justice, he says — no one uses it badly. It is counted among the highest goods that are in the human being himself, together with all the soul's virtues that make up an upright and honorable life. For no one uses prudence, fortitude, or temperance badly. In all of them, as in that justice you just named, RIGHT REASON thrives; without it there are no virtues; and no one can use RIGHT REASON badly.

title: Natural light remains after the Fall; theology assents by God's revealing authority from proximate scriptural principles
english: 12. Nor can it be denied that such reason — such knowledge — still belongs to the human being after the fall. To deny it is to deny the innate notions and the law of nature themselves, and so to contradict the Scriptures, which acknowledge nature's light in theoretical and in practical matters alike.

13. In theoretical matters Scripture confirms that this light and knowledge still remain, so far that what stands first in that order is said to be known naturally in some measure — namely that God is, and that he is cause of all things, just, and the avenger of crimes (see [[Psalm 19:1 >> Bible:Psalm 19:1]]; [[Psalm 19:2 >> Bible:Psalm 19:2]]; Wisdom 13:2; [[Acts 14:16 >> Bible:Acts 14:16]]; [[Acts 17:26 >> Bible:Acts 17:26]]; [[Romans 1:19 >> Bible:Romans 1:19]]–[[Romans 1:21 >> Bible:Romans 1:21]]).

14. In practical matters the sacred writings acknowledge the same light no less clearly ([[Romans 1:32 >> Bible:Romans 1:32]]; [[Romans 2:14 >> Bible:Romans 2:14]]–[[Romans 2:15 >> Bible:Romans 2:15]]; [[1 Corinthians 11:14 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 11:14]]).
15. But in the second kind of discipline — the one named in number 7 — the ground of assent is the authority of God who reveals.
16. Still, both of these grounds are remote. They do not so much enter the discursive chain as stand presupposed before it begins.

17. Philosophers prove their dogmas from proximate principles — physics from physical principles, mathematics from mathematical ones — not from the most general maxim, "Whatever right reason dictates is true." In the same way theologians prove their dogmas from proximate principles, namely from the sayings and oracles of sacred Scripture — not from the remote and most general maxim, "Whatever God reveals is true."

title: The first principle of sacred theology is divine revelation
english: V. The first principle of sacred theology, then, is divine revelation. By it every doubt about religion ends in the mind of a person who is truly Christian, watchful, and through the Holy Spirit earnestly wrestling with his own errors and sins. In that revelation his faith — the faith that makes him a Christian — at last conquers, stands, and is founded. It frees the assenting mind from every fear and suspicion of being deceived, and makes him so sure that he would rather suffer anything than deny what he has once embraced.

The Apostle calls this first principle of theological teaching the illumination of knowledge — φωτισμὸς τῆς γνώσεως ([[2 Corinthians 4:6 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 4:6]]–[[2 Corinthians 4:7 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 4:7]]): For God, who said light should shine out of darkness, has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ. But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may be God's and not from us. Compare [[1 Corinthians 2:4 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:4]] and [[1 Corinthians 2:13 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 2:13]], where sacred analytics are set out for us, and a spiritual, efficacious demonstration is preferred uniquely to the persuasive words of human wisdom.

title: Melanchthon: church doctrine is taken from God's revealed sayings, not from demonstrations
english: And Melanchthon speaks wisely in the preface to the Loci Communes. The doctrine of the church, he says, is not taken from demonstrations, but from sayings that God handed down to the human race by sure and illustrious testimonies — sayings through which, in his immense goodness, he disclosed himself and his will.

Just as philosophy seeks what is certain, separates it from what is uncertain, and names as causes of certainty universal experience, principles, and demonstrations, so in the church's teaching the cause of certainty is the revelation of God, and what must be weighed is which sentences God has handed down.

As any sound mind finds this sentence certain — "Twice four are eight" — because it is natural knowledge, like the knowledge of principles, so let the articles of faith, the divine threats and promises, stand for us certain and unmoved. So let the penitent be certain that sins are remitted, that for the Son of God's sake he is heard, and that he is made an heir of eternal life.

But the causes of certainty differ. The mind sees the sentence about numbers by its own judgment. The articles of faith are certain because of revelation, confirmed by God's sure and illustrious testimonies — the raising of the dead and many other miracles. Yet because these are matters set outside the judgment of the human mind, the assent is weaker: it arises because the mind is moved by those testimonies and miracles and is helped by the Holy Spirit to assent.

title: Certainty rests on the revelation of the truthful God; analytic method serves theology but does not produce justifying faith
english: Philosophy teaches that we should doubt what sense has not ascertained, what is not a principle, and what demonstration has not confirmed. So here one may doubt — or ἐπέχειν, withhold judgment — whether hollowness alone is why the rainbow is an arc. Yet we know that the church's doctrine, handed down by God, is certain and unchangeable, even when sense does not grasp it, even when it is not born with us as principles are, and even when demonstration does not find it. The cause of certainty is the REVELATION OF GOD WHO IS TRUTHFUL.
The Word of God makes us ἀμεταπτώτους — unshaken — in Christian faith with πληροφορία, full assurance, as so many martyrdoms testify.

The analytic method applied to the disciplines — or, more clearly, didactic syllogisms drawn from each discipline's own principles — makes us learned in every kind, knowing and assenting ἀμεταπτώτως. Not only because they have a βιαστικήν, compelling force that drives and convicts τὸν ἔσω λόγον, the inner reason, mind, and conscience, but also because such syllogisms draw their reasons from the proper nature of their subjects — not from accidents or from some common attributes, but from true essentials.

In other disciplines analysis aims at nothing else than this: from vernacular propositions whose predicates have an essential and defining bond with their subjects, it leads us necessarily into knowledge of a necessary and vernacular conclusion. So too in sacred theology the only end of analysis to seek is that, by the help of logic and especially of analytics, we may gain accurate knowledge of theological questions from theology's own λήμμασι — its proper assumptions — and enjoy similar fruits: accurate distinctions between proper and common reasons, and a way of defining spiritual things that logical precepts can supply.

Not the greater gifts, though. Justifying faith is God's alone to give, and the Holy Spirit kindles it in our hearts; likewise the fruits of the Spirit's faith are good works. See the most learned Joachim Camerarius, in the prolegomena to his notation of figures of speech on the four Gospels.

title: Divine revelation is general or special; its object and mode must be considered
english: VI. Divine revelation is of two kinds. One is general, coming from nature ([[Romans 1:19 >> Bible:Romans 1:19]]). The other is special, granted above nature ([[John 17:6 >> Bible:John 17:6]]).
VII. Of this revelation, both the object and the mode must be considered.

title: Some revealed things are known only supernaturally; Scripture also presupposes truths known by nature
english: VIII. That object is the things revealed — either had purely and uniquely from supernatural revelation, or also knowable from elsewhere.

Those called revealed κατ' ἐξοχήν, preeminently, stand apart from other dogmas Scripture contains that the light of nature also knows ([[Romans 1:19 >> Bible:Romans 1:19]]–[[Romans 1:21 >> Bible:Romans 1:21]]; [[Romans 2:14 >> Bible:Romans 2:14]]–[[Romans 2:15 >> Bible:Romans 2:15]]; [[Acts 14:17 >> Bible:Acts 14:17]]; [[Hebrews 11:6 >> Bible:Hebrews 11:6]]). So Theophylact on Hebrews 11: That God is, he says, we hold by faith. Others, following Thomas (Summa I q.2 a.2 ad 1), call that other truth a presupposition of faith and a preamble to the articles of faith.

Scripture presupposes this and the other dogmas of this clause — and the weight of such matters — as known from elsewhere and also to be drawn from nature's light. So they wrong the truth who claim that nature's light conflicts with Scripture, or who think anyone can explain Scripture rightly and sufficiently without secular learning. Otherwise even the unlearned, once they had read and reread the Scriptures, would be great theologians — as certain Anabaptists believe.

The Apostle of the Gentiles himself condemns such men when he expressly appeals to what nature teaches ([[1 Corinthians 11:14 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 11:14]]): ἢ οὐδὲ αὐτὴ ἡ φύσις διδάσκει ὑμᾶς; — Does not nature itself teach you this?

title: As to mode, revelation declares or proves
english: IX. As to mode, divine revelation is either declaring or proving.

The Apostle says in [[Hebrews 1:1 >> Bible:Hebrews 1:1]] that God spoke 'in many portions and in many ways' — polymeros kai polytropos — to the fathers of old, and in these last days has spoken to us in the Son. The modes of divine revelation cannot, it seems, be known with exact precision. On them see Peter Galatinus, On the Secrets of Catholic Truth II.12; Paul Fagius in the Chaldean paraphrase on Exodus 28; and Drusius at the opening of his Commentary on difficult places in Genesis.
X. Declaring revelation is that by which God's will is signified nakedly. Proving revelation is that by which the truth once declared is demonstrated.

title: Revelation is immediate or mediate; immediate revelation is given to God's messengers by secret inspiration
english: XI. Revelation is also immediate or mediate. Immediate revelation belongs generally to the ambassadors; mediate, to those to whom they are sent. I say "generally," because sometimes even those who are not ambassadors receive it for their own instruction — as Joseph did ([[Matthew 1:20 >> Bible:Matthew 1:20]]; [[Matthew 2:13 >> Bible:Matthew 2:13]]; still more, [[Matthew 2:12 >> Bible:Matthew 2:12]]).
XII. Immediate revelation is that by which God disclosed his word to his ambassadors through secret inspiration and set it on their mouth to be announced to others.

title: Immediate revelation without messengers has modes and grades; it comes by signs, spirit, or species
english: Sacred history establishes that God has spoken either through human messengers or without them — that is, without those he himself appointed as messengers — and not in one mode alone ([[Numbers 12:6 >> Bible:Numbers 12:6]]-[[Numbers 12:8 >> Bible:Numbers 12:8]]): "Hear now my words: if there is a prophet of the LORD among you, I make myself known to him by some VISION, or I speak with him by a DREAM. Not so my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house: mouth to mouth I speak with him, and I show him, not in riddles; he beholds the likeness of the LORD." Compare Augustine, On Genesis according to the letter, book 12, chapter 7 and following.

XIII. Divine revelation given to human beings without messengers has diverse modes and grades. Whenever those recipients are so affected that it becomes plain something is being said from God, the spectacle binds them to believe what is said — so strongly that it often drives them to publish it. Compare [[Amos 3:6 >> Bible:Amos 3:6]]-[[Amos 3:7 >> Bible:Amos 3:7]]; [[Jeremiah 20:9 >> Bible:Jeremiah 20:9]].
XIV. This revelation comes by signs, or by spirit, or by species.

XV. By signs: they seize the senses of people asleep or awake — as in a kind of imperfect ecstasy, carried off from ordinary objects — and affect them outwardly or inwardly. This grade may be called sensual. See the scholion on Aphorism 9.

title: By spirit and by species; these two grades may be called intellectual
english: XVI. By spirit: speaking within or without, it teaches the intellect. For examples see [[Acts 8:29 >> Bible:Acts 8:29]] and [[Acts 16:7 >> Bible:Acts 16:7]].

XVII. By species: it immediately transforms the mind once a perfect ecstasy has opened that mind and withdrawn it from the senses. Paul the Apostle supplies a famous instance ([[2 Corinthians 12:2 >> Bible:2 Corinthians 12:2]]). Compare our epilogism On the true religion and the Catholic Church, disputation 10 on prophetic light, and disputation 12 on divine prophecy. These two degrees can be comprehended under one, which we may without inconvenience call intellectual.

title: Mediate revelation; it is manifest or occult; manifest needs no added signs
english: XVIII. Mediate revelation is that by which God, through his ambassadors, signifies to others something that must be believed as divine.
XIX. Mediate revelation is either (1) manifest or occult.

XX. It is manifest when God, through his ambassadors, signifies something as divine to others in such a way that the very mode of the revelation and its circumstances — without any further signs added — make it evident of themselves that God is speaking. So God promulgated his law to the people through Moses ([[Exodus 20 >> Bible:Exodus 20]] and following). The equity of that law is so plain that, even if no signs were added, a holy voice would still cry aloud its divine origin.

title: Occult mediate revelation binds by accompanying signs
english: XXI. It is occult when God, through his ambassadors, signifies something as divine to others and also employs certain signs — signs whose force drives the messengers to announce and binds the hearers to believe. So God, through Moses, confronted Pharaoh with various signs ([[Exodus 7 >> Bible:Exodus 7]]-[[Exodus 10 >> Bible:Exodus 10]]); through Jeremiah he foreshadowed his people's coming ruin by a girdle ([[Jeremiah 13 >> Bible:Jeremiah 13]]). Such is the barber's razor ([[Ezekiel 5:1 >> Bible:Ezekiel 5:1]]); such the marriage with a harlot ([[Hosea 1:2 >> Bible:Hosea 1:2]]).

title: Revelation is unwritten or written; one Word in substance, dual in mode; against a real pontifical distinction
english: XXII. Second: divine revelation is either unwritten or written. Divine things can be known only through God and his word — whether that word is ἄγραφον, unwritten, or ἔγγραφον, written. Whatever is known from it returns to this principle: Whatever God has said must be believed; or, The mouth of the Lord has spoken, therefore it must be believed.

As to the substance of doctrine this Word is altogether one; as to the mode of revelation it is, as it were, twofold — unwritten and written. That mode of revelation is what chiefly needs explanation. Although everything revealed proceeds from one and the same Spirit, not everything is disclosed in the same way. Some things are written; some are gathered by inference — as Gregory Nazianzen teaches in book 5 On Theology, Basil the Great in On the true faith, and Augustine in On Baptism against the Donatists, book 2 chapter 14 and book 4 chapter 23.

Some things are not, and yet are said to be in the Scriptures — that God sits, that he has ears and eyes. Some things are, and yet are not said expressly and in so many words — that the Holy Spirit is God — though something is said from which the point follows of necessity, as when one who says twice five says ten, and one who says twice two says four, even without using those exact words. Some things neither are nor are said. Finally, some both are and are said.

Those who join the papists in setting a real distinction between the written and the unwritten word of God go badly astray. Irenaeus speaks wisely (Against heresies, book 3, chapter 1): We have known the disposition of our salvation through no others than those through whom the Gospel reached us — which they first heralded, and afterwards, by God's will, handed down to us in the Scriptures as the foundation and pillar of our faith to come.

title: Unwritten revelation by living voice; corruption; writing for stability; do not require the unwritten when Scripture is given
english: XXIII. Unwritten revelation is that by which the divine things we must believe are signified by the word handed down with a living voice. By living voice — of God himself, or of angels, or of the holy fathers, prophets, and Apostles — the word of God was once delivered. Human carelessness and Satan's malice corrupted and depraved it in many ways. So God restored and confirmed the purity of his word by fresh revelations from time to time, and at last, for greater stability and certainty, also willed it to be committed to writing.

Here a rule must be noted: once written revelation has been given, the unwritten is not to be demanded rashly, nor forced on others by tyranny — against Coster, Enchiridion of controversies, chapter 1, where he claims Christ willed neither that his Church hang on paper writings nor that mysteries be committed to parchments. See also Bellarmine, On the unwritten word of God, book 4, chapter 3; and Sadeel, Whitaker, and Nigrinus on the papistic contempt of sacred Scripture — indeed Christ himself ([[John 5:39 >> Bible:John 5:39]]; [[John 17 >> Bible:John 17]]) and Paul ([[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]-[[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]).
